1.q: 1. In trading, we want theories that describe how the markets work instead of theories  that impose what the market should do.
2. The application of trading techniques holds many insights that can take years to learn  by yourself. Having access to these insights in explicit form dramatically shortens the  learning curve

2.q: 1. A fractal is a pattern that circles around itself
2. Broad price extremes are separated by many candlesticks while adjacent price  extremes are not.
3. The adjacent market extremes on a lower timeframe are the broad market extremes  on a higher timeframe.

3.q: 1. Intrinsic candlestick properties in absolute terms examine the change from one candle  to the next
2. The presence of extrinsic forces in the market can alter the interpretation of  candlesticks given by the intrinsic properties in both absolute and relative terms
3. Trend phase and price barriers are considered to be extrinsic forces acting on price  action
4. One of the most difficult aspects of price action reading is knowing when to change  perception from broad to narrow and vice versa

4.q: 1. Both volatility and volume are considered to be intrinsic properties of a candlestick
2. The Candle Bias quantifies, and the Body Size qualifies the candle
3. Volatility and Uncertainty are measured by the Range and Body% respectively
4. Shadow symmetry and body position are two sides of the same coin
5. A wide range candle can be objectively observed when its range goes above 2 or 3  standard deviations from the mean in the modified ATR(1) indicator
6. The upper shadow implies bullish pressure, and the lower shadow implies bearish  pressure
7. The body position/shadow symmetry can help contextualize the notion of uncertainty  given by the body%

5.q: 1. Switching timeframes can lead to a paradox where more information creates a worse  analysis
2. Price is less likely to follow the path of least resistance throughout the formation of the  candlestick
3. The ambiguity in candlesticks with very small body and large symmetrical shadows  demonstrates how body% is an important measure of uncertainty

6.q: 1. The meaningful interpretation of candlesticks emerges when the intrinsic properties  are analyzed in context
2. It’s possible that intrinsic properties clash with each other leading to contradictory  interpretations
3. The importance of intrinsic properties becomes more evident when more complex  candlesticks are analyzed

7.q: 1. Relative intrinsic properties relate to the analysis of candlesticks in isolation
2. Range dynamics must be contextualized by body% and shadow symmetry
3. The simple geometry of candlesticks yields complex interpretations once we start to  analyze the evolution of candles over time
4. The precise analysis of intrinsic properties in absolute and relative terms must be  performed in all candlesticks

8.q: 1. The location of a candlestick relative to the overall trend doesn’t alter its interpretation
3. A continuation divergence tends to be stronger than a reversal divergence because it  has the trend on its side
4. Larger length between price extremes tends to lead to a weaker divergence signal
5. There is no such thing as fractal volume
1. A price barrier can modulate the interpretation we get from the intrinsic properties of  a candlestick
2. The outer lines of the Bollinger Bands indicator are examples of barriers that are  traditional, geometric, and sloped
3. A decelerated price movement by itself is ambiguous, but if it seems to be held by a  barrier, there is a tendency of observing a reversal instead of a continuation
4. Accelerated price movements seem to be powerful, but they actually imply a loss of  power in price action, and that’s why they are considered an exhaustion
5. Decelerated price movements seem to be a loss of power, but not necessarily. Price  can be reaccumulating energy

9.q: 1. The roughness of price is directly proportional to its fractal dimension
2. The Coastline Paradox in fractal geometry shows us that the interpretation of price is  objective and subjective at the same time
3. A rough price vector in one timeframe is necessarily rough in all timeframes
4. The perception of fractal dimension can point to the optimal timeframe to trade a  specific price vector
5. Price action reverses significantly when flows of different sizes align

10.q: 1. Frequency lines are born when we overlay fractal analysis onto traditional support and  resistance lines
2. In a downward price vector, the lower frequencies point to reversals and the upper  frequencies point to continuations
3. Real-time frequencies eventually become historical frequencies

11.q: 1. The butterfly effect is a feature of chaotic systems
2. Financial markets are chaotic, but not fractal
3. The more reliable dynamic frequency breakouts tend to happen with low to medium  volatility as it can be objectively measured with the ATR(1)

12.q: 1. There are mainly two types of manipulation patterns that form all of the fractal  variations
2. The combination of broad and fractal manipulations is called self-similar manipulation
3. All fractal candles imply a fractal manipulation, but not all fractal manipulations imply a  fractal candle
4. In fractal manipulations, bearish signals can end up being part of a bullish signal and  vice versa

13.q: 1. All fractal candles imply a fractal manipulation and vice versa
2. There is a wide array of fractal candles with various degrees of reliability once we  consider the intrinsic properties and extrinsic forces of the market
3. The higher the level of integration in a fractal candle, the greater its reliability, but the  lower its frequency
4. Fractal candles occurring in upward or downward progression imply a dissonance in  terms of velocity divergence when we consider both sides of range dynamics

14.q: 1. The LRC is a fractal barrier because it is calculated numerically while being grounded  geometrically
2. Even though LRCs are fractal barriers, we can use them in either fractal or non-fractal  ways
3. You can draw LRCs effectively in any moment
4. There is a lot of benefit in combining LRCs with Pitchforks since they provide non obvious angles and barriers in the chart
5. The LRC cannot make use of overthrow and underthrow lines

15.q: 1. There is confusion in technical analysis because some behavioral tools have a  mathematical connotation despite being mathematically invalid
2. A self-fulfilling prophecy effect can confirm a false belief
3. Behavioral patterns in isolation tend to work as repellers
4. The integration of behavioral/economic tools and mathematical/physical tools can  generate self-reinforcing scenarios with good precision and timing
5. The Andrews Pitchfork and the LRC are both Economic Tools

16.q: 1. Trading is a stochastic game, meaning that the outcome is a function of skill and  chance simultaneously
2. Trading is a game of incomplete and asymmetric information, unknown and variable  probabilities
3. Information is a critical aspect in trading because traders cannot rely completely on the  feedback they get from the market in order to learn
4. The higher the level of integration the lower the difficulty
5. The higher the level of integration, the greater the reliability of a trade although it can  never reach 100% reliability
6. The lower the timeframe, the easier integration tends to be

17.q: 1. Trading is like a playing a game in an arena where diverse games are being played in  such a way that the games affect each other
2. Doing the right thing in trading is guarantee that success will be obtained
3. There are right ways of losing and wrong ways of winning, and this knowledge depends  on knowing how markets and trading work
4. It’s better to learn how to reward behavior rather than performance because the  former is more under the trader’s control
5. It’s a bad idea trying to retail trade for a living because trading performance cannot  provide enough financial stability for short term recurrent goals
6. Trading is especially addictive for a trader who is unaware of the behavioral and  mathematical pitfalls associated with it
7. There are ways of using the addictive quality of trading against itself in a productive  way

18.q: 1. In the top-down approach, the trader begins with the broader aspect of the extrinsic  forces and then narrows the analysis down to the intrinsic properties.
2. High quality trading is more about patience and strategic action than blind and  constant action
3. You’ll be constantly tempted to act based on trade signals in isolation. You must resist  this urge and remember that high quality trades require context
4. Doing the right thing doesn’t guarantee that your trade will be successful because  trading is a stochastic game

19.q: 1. The appearance of a trade trigger without the appropriate integration of techniques  means you should act on it right away
2. Limit triggers can increase precision at the expense of being more difficult and also at  the risk of not getting filled
3. A stop loss must be placed above/below the potentially newly formed market extreme

20.q: 1. A higher return is necessarily a better return
2. The goal of risk management is to overcome the uncertainty of the market in the long  term
3. Traders want to maximize risk while minimizing returns
4. A trader can make money only by using risk management

21.q: 1. Favorable ratios are the ones where risk and reward are equal
2. There is no mathematical edge in different risk-reward ratios if trades are opened  randomly
3. As ratios increase linearly, the additional benefit in margin of error decays  exponentially

22.q: 1. Phase-dependent ratios mean that the optimal ratio depends on the market scenario
2. It’s possible to produce 100% win rate in the long term
3. The alignment between market analysis and risk management allows the edge to  emerge in risk-reward ratios
4. Ideally, you want to enter trades with favorable ratios in the presence of the butterfly  effect and near repellers

23.q: 1. Loss aversion means that we prefer avoiding losses over obtaining equivalent wins
2. Psychologically speaking, to offset loss aversion we need to use a ratio between 1.5  and 2.5
4. Favorable ratios are uncomfortable in the present, but they are sustainable.  Unfavorable ratios are comfortable in the present, but they lead to destruction

24.q: 1. Risk-reward ratios should be phase-dependent and favorably unbounded
2. Boundedness means that ratios depend on market phase
3. The ability to analyze the market properly and the capacity to delay gratification are  critical for risk management to work

25.q: 1. A trader can increase the %risk per trade if he uses proper risk-reward ratios
2. %Risk should be low enough, so you don’t care about a large losing streak. This level  will certainly be equal or less than 1% per trade
3. Position sizing models that grow capital faster do that at the expense of increasing risk,  and therefore, decreasing sustainability
4. The higher the leverage, the higher the risk, and therefore, the lower the sustainability  of returns

26.q: 1. It’s dangerous to think in terms of return without considering the risk associated to  obtain such return
2. The goal of trading your own capital is long term wealth generation, capitalizing on the  power of compounding
3. Winning streaks can be sustained for a long time, and losing streaks are avoidable
4. The trader cannot properly judge performance against itself (subjectively) because  variations in performance are not only a product of variations in skill
5. Benchmarking and opportunity cost are fundamental aspects of objective performance  measurement
6. The goal of trading is to grow capital as fast as possible
7. The Sharpe Ratio measures the quality of the trader’s return, and it must be compared  with the Sharpe Ratio of the benchmark
8. A higher return is always a better return
9. If you find an “edge”, you can certainly lose it
10. Past performance is not indicative of future results partly because the probability of  techniques and patterns vary over time

27.q: 1. Signal alternation in fractal overextension signals can lead to contradictory conclusions
2. The best part of behavioral trading techniques such as Elliott Wave theory is the  simplest part of the theory
3. LRCs and Pitchforks are mutually exclusive

28.q: 2. Trades at the beginning of a trend should aim for higher ratios
3. The integration of nonobvious patterns points to fundamental properties of price  action that are unrelated to a self-fulfilling prophecy effect
4. Certain barriers like AR lines and pitchforks allow us to see price using a physics-based  approach while LRCs allow us to see price using a mathematical approach
5. All significant price reversals have fractal candles or manipulations patterns

29.q: 1. Price action with a higher fractal dimension is easier to trade
2. There are psychological traps involved even in trading price action in a low fractal  dimension
3. The Fractal Price Action Reading Framework exists to help you maintain the necessary  balance between broad and hyper focused analysis
4. By efficiently using the Fractal Price Action Reading Framework, you can avoid losses

30.q: 1. A fractal candle must have all the elements of integration to be reliable
2. Sometimes it’s difficult to find pitchforks that align with the LRCs
3. A good trade can have elements going against it as long as the elements going for it are  stronger
4. Observing signal alternation and width between extremes is not essential in  overextension signals
5. Even in price action with higher fractal dimension we can find useful fractal elements  like self-similar manipulations

31.q: 1. Accelerated price movements give the impression that price is gaining power, but often  times that is misleading. Price exhausts its energy quicker in that setting

2. Theoretically, Feigenbaum ratios have a greater explanatory power in comparison to  Fibonacci ratios since they are a mathematical constant found in chaotic systems.  However, the instances where Feigenbaum ratios can be used in a price chart are quite  limited
3. LRCs are a more reliable way of applying chaos theory to price charts
4. Not being able to delay gratification in a trade is not a problem
5. Fib ratios in the context of Elliott Wave are an example of how phase analysis and price  barriers can be interconnected

32.q: 1. A perfect trade setup means you can increase risk
2. It’s important to understand the origin of the techniques you use in order to trust them
3. Low fractal dimension is a favorable scenario, but it doesn’t mean it’s perfect
4. Subtle changes in price action are difficult to see when you have already formed a bias  for a trade idea
5. A DFB in low fractal dimension can never fail

33.q: 1. The common ground or integration between phase analysis methods can help reduce  the ambiguity that arises in several market scenarios
2. A dynamic target can dramatically increase the final risk-reward ratio, but it requires  the use of more advanced tools
3. Peak performance in one trade is more important than the iteration of trades over  time
4. A sideways market can be ambiguous under the light of Wyckoff’s method alone

34.q: 1. The phase-dependence element of risk-reward ratios can be a critical factor in  triggering a trade
2. It’s possible to find a 5 wave and 3 wave pattern in the same price vector depending on  how you look at it
3. Waiting for confirmation is safer at the expense of being less precise
4. Pitchforks cannot work well with limit orders in market edges

35.q: 1. The Anchored VWAP is a fractal tool because it incorporates geometric and numerical  elements
2. The alignment between strong behavioral patterns and precise mathematical/physical  tools is the sweet spot between power and precision
3. The absence of divergence in one oscillator means that there is the absence of  divergence in all other oscillators

36.q: 1. The best a technical trader can do is to look for areas with the greatest number of  intersecting techniques in the chart
2. Areas where multiple intersections occur are always obvious
3. The Volume Profile Tool can serve as a way to find support/resistance levels

37.q: 1. Hyper integration is the combination of various tools within one type of market  analysis
2. There is an implicit geometry in price action that can be unveiled by the pitchfork and  the linear regression channel
3. The volume profile, the anchored VWAP, Cumulative Volume Delta and VSA are all  important and useful volume tools
4. An apparently unimportant price level can become important if there are enough  elements being integrated in it

38.q: 1. Phase analysis plays an important role in determining if supply/demand zones will hold
2. One of the most important aspects of intrinsic properties is their capacity to show if  price is reacting to a price barrier as expected
3. A major supply/demand zone can be drawn using the DFB and DFS lines in the middle  of a price vector
4. The minor flow of highs and lows changes before the major flow of highs and lows

39.q: 1. A trade idea with simple integration elements necessarily implies in a simple entry
2. Phase analysis methods can generate many ambiguous scenarios
3. Simple lines and channels are self-fulfilling because not a lot of traders can see them
4. The reliability of future price reactions to pitchfork lines is associated with the quality  of price reactions to pitchfork lines in the past

40.q: 1. Decelerating price movement necessarily implies unsustainability
2. A DFB is a sign that price is reversing especially after it reacts to a level where multiple  barriers intersect
3. A common resistance line is a mathematical barrier

41.q: 1. Sometimes, waiting for price confirmation means that the trade entry will become  invalid
2. An integrated fractal candle means that the fractal candle shows reversal divergence in  a lower timeframe
3. The greater the number of elements in a fractal candle, the lower its level of  integration
4. If the trade is well into profitable territory, and the market gives you reasons to  invalidate the currently profitable trade, you can move the stop to breakeven
